title: Roots: What a Chord Is Built On
intro: Every chord is built on one note, its root, and is named after it: C major is built on C, A minor on A, G7 on G. Knowing the root is the key to naming chords, reading chord symbols and finding shapes on the guitar and piano. This page explains what the root is, how to find it, and how it differs from the bass note.

blocks.text: The root is the note the chord is stacked on

Chords in Western music are built by stacking thirds: start on a note, skip one letter, take the next, skip one, take the next. Start on C: C, (skip D) E, (skip F) G. The note you started on, C, is the root. The next is the third (a third above the root) and the next the fifth (a fifth above the root). Together, root–third–fifth is a triad (see Chords (#/arts/music-theory/chords)).

items: C–E–G: root C, so it is a C chord (C major).
A–C–E: root A, an A chord (A minor).
G–B–D–F: root G, a G chord (G seventh, G7). Add one more third to a triad and you get a seventh chord; the root is still the bottom of the stack.

blocks.text: The chord's letter name is always its root. The rest of the name tells you the quality: 'm' means a minor third above the root, '7' adds a seventh, and so on. So when you read 'F♯m', the root is F♯.

items: Step 1. Put your right thumb on middle C. Play C, skip D, play E with finger 3, skip F, play G with finger 5. That is a C major chord; C, under your thumb, is the root.
Step 2. Keep the same hand shape and move it so your thumb is on D: D–F–A. The root is now D, and the chord is D minor.
Step 3. Do the same starting on every white key: E–G–B (E minor), F–A–C (F major), G–B–D (G major), A–C–E (A minor), B–D–F (B diminished). The root is always under your thumb.
Step 4. Use Step ▶ in the keyboard below to walk through these seven chords one at a time. Each key that lights up first in the chord, the lowest one, is the root.

blocks.text: Root and bass are not always the same note

The bass is simply the lowest note sounding. When the root is in the bass, the chord is in root position, the most stable sound. When another chord note is in the bass, the chord is inverted: C–E–G with E at the bottom is still a C chord (root C) but in first inversion; with G at the bottom, second inversion (see Inversions (#/arts/music-theory/chords/inversions)). Chord symbols show this with a slash: C/E means 'C chord, E in the bass'.

To find the root of a chord whose notes are scrambled, rearrange them so they stack in thirds; the bottom of that stack is the root. Example: E–G–C. Rearranged in thirds: C–E–G. Root C, and since E was lowest, it is C/E, first inversion.

widget.title: C major with each chord note in the bass (the root stays C)

blocks.text: On the guitar the root of a chord shape is usually its lowest string that is played, and it is the string you strum from. In the chord diagrams on these pages the root is drawn in red.

items: Step 1. Play an open C chord (x32010): ring finger on string 5 fret 3. That note is C, the root. Strum from string 5 down, never string 6.
Step 2. Play an open G chord (320003): string 6 fret 3 is G, the root. Strum all six strings.
Step 3. Play an open D chord (xx0232): the open string 4 is D, the root. Strum only the top four strings; a bass note below the root would muddy it.

Step 4. Barre chords make the root easy: in an E-shape barre chord the root is under your first finger on string 6; in an A-shape barre chord, under your first finger on string 5. Move the shape until that finger is on the note you want (see The Fretboard (#/arts/guitar/guitar-theory/fretboard) for the note names).
Step 5. Use Step ▶ on the fretboard below: the first step of each example plays just the root, the next strums the chord.

items: Naming: the root gives the chord its letter.
Function: Roman numerals name chords by the scale degree of their root (in C major, a chord with root G is V; see Harmony (#/arts/music-theory/harmony)).
Bass lines: bassists play mostly roots, because the root in the bass makes the harmony clear.
Moving shapes: on guitar, finding the root on string 6 or 5 is how you find any barre chord.

blocks.title: Find the root
blocks.text: What is the root of each chord: (a) A–C♯–E, (b) F–A–D, (c) B–D–G, (d) D–F♯–A–C?
solution: (a) Already stacked in thirds: root A (A major).
(b) Restack: D–F–A. Root D (D minor, with F in the bass: Dm/F).
(c) Restack: G–B–D. Root G (G major with B in the bass: G/B).

blocks.title: Root on the guitar
blocks.text: Where is the root of an A-shape barre chord at the 5th fret, and which chord is it?
solution: In the A shape the root is on string 5 under the first finger. String 5 fret 5 is D (A, A♯, B, C, C♯, D at frets 0–5). So it is a D major chord.
